lesson.title: Writing clear sentences
lesson.objective: Write simple sentences with capital letters and full stops.

objectives: Write simple sentences with capital letters and full stops.
successCriteria: Starts every sentence with a capital letter

items.prompt: Rewrite correctly: "my brother likes tea"

outcomes.studyNotes: A sentence is a group of words that tells us one idea. Every sentence starts with a capital letter, for example: The sun is hot. The word I is always a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence: Today I am happy. Names of people and places also start with a capital letter: Sara, London. At the end of a statement we write a full stop (.). If the sentence is a question we write a question mark (?). Before you finish, check three things: capital at the start, capital for I, and a full stop at the end.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. The word I is always a capital letter.
hints: Look at the first letter of your sentence. Is it a capital?
Look at the very end of the sentence. What mark is missing?
Check the word I. It must be a capital letter too.
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that is correct. Good capital letter and full stop.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the first letter, the word I and the end of the sentence.
scriptedTutor.closing: Well done. Capital at the start, full stop at the end.

outcomes.title: Linking ideas with and, but, because
outcomes.objective: Join two ideas in one written sentence using and (addition), but (contrast) and because (reason).
prerequisites: Can write a simple sentence with a subject and a verb

misconceptions.exampleWrong: The bag is small and it is very heavy.

misconceptions.description: Puts a full stop before the linking word and makes a fragment
misconceptions.exampleWrong: I went to bed early. Because I was tired.

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses and to add an idea
Uses but to show a contrast
Uses because to give a reason in the same sentence

lesson.objective: Join two short sentences with and, but or because.

objectives: Join two short sentences with and, but or because.
successCriteria: Uses and to add an idea
Uses but to show a contrast
Uses because to give a reason in the same sentence

outcomes.studyNotes: We use linking words to join two short sentences into one longer sentence. Use "and" to add another idea: I play tennis and I play chess. Use "but" when the second idea is different or surprising: The test was easy but I made a mistake. Use "because" to give a reason: We stay inside because it is cold. Do not put a full stop before the linking word. Write the whole idea as one sentence and put the full stop at the very end. A comma before "but" is optional at this level.

scriptedTutor.explanation: We use and to add, but to show contrast and because to give a reason. Keep everything in one sentence with one full stop at the end.
hints: Ask: is the second idea an addition, a contrast or a reason?
Is the second idea the opposite of the first? Then think about but.
Do not put a full stop before the linking word.
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that is correct. The linking word fits the meaning.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Think about the meaning: addition, contrast or reason?
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. And adds, but contrasts, because gives a reason.

outcomes.title: Word order in simple sentences
outcomes.objective: Write statements in the order subject + (frequency word) + verb + object + place/time.
prerequisites: Knows what a subject and a verb are

misconceptions.description: Puts the verb at the end, after the object
misconceptions.exampleWrong: Ben a book reads every night.

misconceptions.description: Puts the frequency word (always, never, often) after the verb

teachingSuccessCriteria: Puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object
Puts always/usually/never before the main verb

lesson.title: Making sentences in order
lesson.objective: Order words correctly in a simple English statement.

objectives: Order words correctly in a simple English statement.
successCriteria: Puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object
Puts always/usually/never before the main verb
Puts place or time at the end
grammar: frequency adverbs before the main verb
examples: We usually have lunch at one.

items.prompt: Put in order: "plays / Sam / chess / on Mondays"
Put in order: "usually / we / lunch / have"
Put in order: "often / my aunt / tea / makes"

outcomes.studyNotes: English statements follow a fixed order: subject, verb, object. Example: Sam (subject) plays (verb) football (object). Place and time words usually go at the end: Sam plays football in the park on Fridays. Words like always, usually, often, sometimes and never go before the main verb: We usually have lunch at one. They do not go after the verb. The object does not go before the verb in English. To check a sentence, ask: Who? Then what do they do? Then what or where or when?

scriptedTutor.explanation: In English the order is subject, then verb, then object. Frequency words like always and never go before the main verb. Place and time go at the end.
hints: Find the subject first. Who does the action?
Put the verb straight after the subject.
Words like always or never go before the verb.
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, the word order is correct.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check: subject, then verb, then object, with place or time at the end.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Subject, verb, object, and frequency words before the verb.

lesson.title: Starting and finishing an email
lesson.objective: Write the opening and closing of a short email to a friend or teacher.

objectives: Write the opening and closing of a short email to a friend or teacher.
successCriteria: Opens with Dear/Hi/Hello + the name + a comma
Uses Dear in a formal email to a teacher or manager

outcomes.studyNotes: An email has three parts: an opening, a message and a closing. The opening is a greeting, the name and a comma: Hi Ben, or Dear Ben, For a teacher or a manager we use Dear: Dear Mr Cook, or Dear Mrs Lee, Then we write the message in short clear sentences. The closing is a short phrase, a comma and our name on the next line. With friends: Best wishes, All the best, See you soon, Take care. In a formal email: Kind regards, Best regards, Yours sincerely. Do not only write Thanks or Bye, and do not forget the commas.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Start with a greeting, the name and a comma. Finish with a closing phrase, a comma and your own name. Use Dear for formal emails.
hints: How does your email begin? Add a greeting and the reader's name with a comma.
How does your email end? Add a closing phrase such as Best wishes, then your name.
Is this email formal? Then begin with Dear.
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that is correct. Good opening and closing.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the greeting, the name, the commas and the closing phrase.

outcomes.studyNotes: When we write a list of three or more things, we use commas to separate them. We do not use a comma between only two things: I like tea and coffee. For three or more, write a comma after each item except the last two, which are joined with and: I bought bread, milk and butter. Some writers also put a comma before and (bread, milk, and butter). Both are fine, but be consistent. Never put a comma after and. Do not put commas inside one item: a red hat is one item, not a, red, hat. End the sentence with a full stop.

scriptedTutor.explanation: In a list, put a comma between the items and write and before the last item. Do not put a comma after and.
hints: Count the items in the list. How many are there?
Put a comma after each item before the last two items.
Join the last two items with and, with no comma after and.
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, the commas are in the right places.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check where the commas go in the list.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Commas between items, and before the last one.

objectives: Write a paragraph with a topic sentence and supporting sentences.
successCriteria: Opens with a topic sentence that states the main idea

items.prompt: Write one supporting sentence for the topic "Walking is good for you". Start with For example.

outcomes.studyNotes: A paragraph is a group of sentences about ONE main idea. The first sentence is the topic sentence. It tells the reader the main idea: Sleep is important for good health. The next sentences are supporting sentences. They give reasons, facts or examples, and often begin with phrases like for example, for instance, because or also. A paragraph should have at least three sentences. Do not begin with a small personal detail and do not stop after one sentence. Plan: 1) main idea, 2) reason, 3) example, 4) extra point or short ending. Check that every sentence is about the main idea.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Start with a topic sentence that states your main idea. Then add supporting sentences with reasons and examples, using words like because, for example and also.
hints: What is the one main idea? Put it in your first sentence.
Add a reason with because.
Add an example with for example.
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that is a clear paragraph.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Is the main idea in your first sentence, and do you have supporting sentences?
scriptedTutor.closing: Well done. Main idea first, then reasons and examples.

outcomes.studyNotes: To describe a person we talk about appearance and personality. For features we use has or has got after he, she or one person: She has long hair. He has got blue eyes. We do not say "She have". For height, age and character we use is with an adjective: He is tall. She is friendly and funny. Do not mix them: we say "is tall" but "has long hair". Useful words: hair (short, long, curly), eyes (brown, green), tall, short, young, old, kind, quiet, shy, clever. Begin each sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Use has or has got for things a person has, like hair or eyes. Use is with an adjective for how a person is, like tall or kind. After he or she, say has, not have.

Is this a quality, like kind? Then use is.
With he or she we say has, not have.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check has/is: has for features, is for qualities.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Has for features, is for qualities.

outcomes.title: Formal and informal register
outcomes.objective: Rewrite messages for the right reader: formal (polite phrases, no slang or contractions) for a boss or stranger, informal for a friend.
prerequisites: Can write correct sentences and short emails
Knows polite words like please and thank you

misconceptions.description: Keeps slang, abbreviations, contractions or exclamation marks in a formal message
misconceptions.exampleWrong: Hey, can u fix the heater asap?

misconceptions.description: Thinks formal means blunt: states a demand with I want or an order
misconceptions.exampleWrong: I want the heater fixed now.

teachingSuccessCriteria: Replaces slang and abbreviations with full standard words
Avoids contractions in formal writing

lesson.title: Choosing the right tone
lesson.objective: Rewrite a message so the tone fits the reader, formal or informal.

objectives: Rewrite a message so the tone fits the reader, formal or informal.
successCriteria: Replaces slang and abbreviations with full standard words
Avoids contractions in formal writing
Makes requests polite with could you / I would be grateful / I would like to
Switches formal wording to relaxed wording for a friend
grammar: modal requests: could you, would you
examples: Informal: Can you call me later? Formal: Could you please call me later?
Informal: I'm sorry, I can't come. Formal: I regret that I am unable to attend.

items.prompt: Rewrite formally: "Can you give me a call?"
acceptedAnswers: Could you please give me a call?

items.prompt: Rewrite informally: "I would be grateful for your help."
Rewrite formally: "Gonna send it asap, ok?"
acceptedAnswers: I will send it as soon as possible.
I am going to send it as soon as possible.
targetForms: I will send it as soon as possible.

outcomes.studyNotes: Register means how formal or informal our language is. Use formal language with a manager, a teacher or a stranger. Use informal language with friends and family. Formal: no slang (hey, mate, gonna), no abbreviations (asap, u, thx), no contractions (I am, cannot, do not) and no exclamation marks. Requests are polite and indirect: Could you please send me the file? I would be grateful if you could help. I would like to ask about the date. I am writing to say that. Do not use blunt wording such as "I want" or "Send it". Informal: contractions, short phrases and friendly words are fine: Can you lend me a pen? Thanks!

scriptedTutor.explanation: Formal writing has no slang, no abbreviations, no contractions and uses polite request phrases such as could you or I would like to. Informal writing is relaxed and short, like a text to a friend.
hints: Who is the reader? A boss or a friend?
For formal writing, remove slang and short forms and write the full words.
Make the request polite: Could you...? or I would like to...
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, the tone is right for the reader.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the reader and the tone: slang, contractions and polite phrases.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Match your language to your reader.
